newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania rebels shun amnesty, West urges dialogue.
newsitem.headline: Albania rebels shun amnesty, West urges dialogue.

text.p: Armed rebels in southern Albania dismissed an amnesty offer from President Sali Berisha on Friday and refused to lay down arms while the West urged him not to relaunch a military campaign against them.
Rebel committees in the Adriatic towns of Sarande and Vlore, where rioting and looting broke out last weekend, said they would not surrender their arms until Berisha stepped down.

"We're not giving up our weapons until Berisha resigns," Fuat Karali, a former police officer and now a member of Sarande's rebel council told a mass rally in the town square witnessed by a Reuters reporter.

Delegations from the European Union and Council of Europe, intensifying efforts to end two months of violence, welcomed a two-day suspension of a military drive against the insurgents decreed by Berisha and appealed against any new use of force.
A delegation of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, led by former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, was due on Saturday.
"I urged the president to postpone as long as possible or refrain from violence," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo told a news conference after three hours of talks with Berisha.
"I repeatedly said: 'Make it possible for the European Union to help Albania'."

Van Mierlo told Berisha the EU favoured fresh elections and a new constitution and said the president was considering such an approach. He said it was up to Albanians to decide whether they wanted change through a new broader-based government or initially through an interim administration.

At least 16 people have died in the past week in the latest wave of two months of violence, sparked initially by the collapse of fraudulent investment funds. Parliament, dominated by Berisha's Democratic Party, proclaimed emergency rule last weekend and then re-elected the president to a five-year term.
In Sarande, a town of some 15,000 people on the Adriatic coast, visible from the Greek holiday island of Corfu, rebels set up barricades in apparent preparation for a long siege.
The message appeared the same from the port of Vlore, 160 km (110 miles) north of Sarande.
"They said the amnesty will not satisfy them. They want President Berisha to resign and they want their money back," a Western reporter who reached the town told Reuters by telephone.

Nearly half of Vlore's 80,000 people, as well as hundreds of thousands of other people across the country of 3.4 million, had invested their savings in pyramid investment schemes which crumbled in January.

The demise of pyramid schemes at the beginning of the year sparked weeks of protests which erupted into anarchy last weekend as rioters went on the rampage, seizing arms from police and army depots and looting shops.
The suspension of military activity, decreed by Berisha after talks with political parties, offered insurgents an amnesty if they surrendered their arms by six a.m. (0500 GMT) on Sunday.

In Tirana, a four-member mission of the Council of Europe called on all parties to condemn the insurgency and urged the main opposition Socialist Party to take up the seats it won in parliament last year in a disputed general election.

"All political parties should state their condemnation of acts of criminal violence and rebellion in southern Albania if these should persist despite the March 6 offer of an amnesty," the mission said in a statement.

Albania is a member of the 40-state Council of Europe, set up to promote democracy and human rights. The mission urged the government to respect the European Human Rights Convention and end restrictions on the domestic media.
